bullets.text: A transformer fire at the Vellmore substation on July 8, 2025 triggered a cascading grid failure that left an estimated 1.9 million customers across the Grayford metro area without power during a record heat wave.
The blackout halted the Grayford Metro with three trains stranded in tunnels, knocked out traffic signals citywide, degraded mobile networks, and cut water pressure to high-rise buildings.

Two deaths were linked to the blackout — a collision at a darkened interchange and a heat-related death in an unrestored high-rise — and 41 people were treated for heat or entrapment-related conditions.

Supply was fully restored after roughly 54 hours via rerouted feeds and a mobile transformer, and the mayor announced an independent inquiry into the failure and the restoration communication problems.
A large fire breaks out at the Vellmore substation; protective shutdowns begin cutting power across Grayford.
Grayford Metro suspends all lines with three trains stopped in tunnels; fire crews respond to dozens of elevator entrapments.
The airport switches to backup power and halts departures for about 90 minutes; Ridgeway Memorial Hospital runs on generators.
Three metro trains carrying 380 passengers were stranded in tunnels between stations.
All 380 stranded metro passengers were evacuated through the tunnels via controlled walkway evacuations.
Fire crews worked through dozens of elevator entrapment calls.
An estimated 1.9 million customers lost power across the Grayford metro area, with the cascade taking minutes from first trip to metro-wide blackout.
The Grayford Metro suspended all lines; the airport halted departures for about 90 minutes and suffered evening-long delays.
Traffic signals failed citywide, causing gridlock and requiring police control at 40 major intersections.
Controlled evacuations moved 380 passengers along tunnel walkways from three stranded metro trains.
The primary hazard was the loss of electricity for up to 54 hours during a record heat wave, making heat exposure the leading threat to life.
Secondary hazards included darkened intersections, elevator and tunnel entrapments, high-rise water loss, and cold-chain risk to medicines.
Fire crews extinguished the substation fire and cleared dozens of elevator entrapments; police controlled traffic at 40 major intersections.
Authorities told drivers to treat all dark signals as four-way stops and warned against forcing elevator doors.
Water customers were advised to fill containers pre-emptively and later to flush taps before drinking.
Early reactions mixed confusion and alarm at the scale of the outage with concern about the heat.
